name: Pedro Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to any company, union or party, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Northpoint Creative, seven of us in an office over a dentist. We do brochures, sale boards and website banners for estate agents and two local housebuilders. A normal day is cleaning up property photos, laying out a brochure for a three-bed semi, and making the same banner in six sizes. Twice a week I go out with the camera and shoot flats myself, which is my favourite part.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Speed, mostly. Tunde, our senior designer, can do a brochure in an hour and it takes me half a day. Claire, who owns the place, is patient, but I know I'm still the slow one. I use an AI tool now and then to clean up skies in photos, because everyone else does and it saves twenty minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was a bit overblown. It's a decent tool for photo cleanup and that's about it. I'd say that over a beer after football and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's tied to houses selling, not to AI, and estate agents cut their brochure budgets first when the market's slow. We had a quiet spring this year. So I'm not panicking, but I'm not relaxed either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, try to get faster so Tunde stops doing my brochures for me, and keep about four months saved. I might pay for a short photography course, because the shoots are the part clients compliment. That's maybe three hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, which is how I've felt since the spring. Nothing to do with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the property market affect Northpoint?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When sales slow, the agents order fewer brochures and ask for cheaper ones. This spring Claire told us there'd be no pay rises and no new hires. Nobody lost a job, but I noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cook more and skip the weekend away. I live alone in a studio flat, so the rent is all mine, and that's the bill I watch. I've got enough for about four months if it came to it.

I'd say it **over a beer** after football and move on.
think: My job is tied to **houses selling**, not to AI.
A **quiet spring** meant no pay rises or new hires at Northpoint.
do: Get faster so **Tunde** stops redoing his brochures.
Pay about **300** for a short photography course.
Keep about **four months** of rent saved.
feel: A little **uneasy**, as he has been since the spring.

steps.text: Practise brochure layouts to catch up with Tunde's speed
Take a short property photography course for about 300

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and I'd mean it for myself too. Estate agents will want brochures in ten minutes, and whoever does that cheapest wins. I'm not going to complain about it online, there's no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the brochures and banners are the first thing to go. An estate agent will be able to drop photos into a tool and get a brochure out, and they won't need an agency like Northpoint for that. The shoots last longer, because somebody has to be in the flat with the camera.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, once I'd seen Tunde use them, and get good at checking what they spit out. I'd push to do more shoots and maybe video walkthroughs of houses. And I'd raise my savings from four months to six by skipping the trip to see my brother next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a practical way. I've got some time, and some of my job is out of the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the AI tools now and then. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd use them every day, but not first. I like to watch someone else make the mistakes before I try something. Tunde would probably be the one to show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Northpoint?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Megan, who does the website banners and social posts. That's all screen work and it's what the tools do best. Tunde's okay because clients ask for him, and Claire owns the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need some kind of help, quickly, because nobody can retrain in two years. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign things. Mostly I'd be talking to friends about who's hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Northpoint's design work is gone by 2028. The shoots might last until 2031, when robots can walk around a flat with a camera. So I'd have three years of being a photographer, which is a strange way to start a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd cut everything to the bone and move savings toward six months. I'd go out and look for photography work with bigger estate agents directly, and ask Claire if I could go part-time while I build it. And I'd look at anything hands-on near me, like a builder's site office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Four months of rent in the bank feels like nothing when your whole field disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the shoots. Do they still help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. Somebody still has to open the door, set up the lights and walk through a flat. But estate agents could do that themselves with a phone and an AI that fixes the photos, so it's not a sure thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother works in a warehouse, and I'd tell him he's got a few more years than me, which is funny because he always said I had the cushy job. I'd probably ask if I could stay with him for a bit if the rent got too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so people should be planning, and the government should be too. I'd be sensible about it, not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my design work probably goes before full AGI does, maybe by 2029. But five years is enough to build the photography side properly while I still get a salary. Robots by 2034 means maybe four or five good years of shoots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take the photography course and start doing weekend shoots for estate agents on my own. I'd stay at Northpoint full-time while it lasts. I'd keep saving and maybe look at in-house design at one of the housebuilders, since big firms are slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. It feels like I could actually get somewhere before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five years enough for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, daily by then. I'd be the one checking the AI's brochures for wrong room sizes, which it gets wrong all the time. That might keep me useful for a year or two longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. In the fast version of AGI I don't get to try anything, but five years is enough to try two things and see which one sticks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's not panic. People should start learning things now, but calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, I think. I'd lose the brochure work eventually but I'd be thirty-seven, with years of photography and maybe a house of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see how the tools actually change things before doing anything big. I'd keep saving and do the photography course. I might buy a better camera once I knew the shoots were paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. It's far enough away to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy property photography gear and build a name with the agents slowly. In the fast versions I'd be scrambling, here I'd be choosing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of it worry you, with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The housing market, honestly, more than AI. If houses don't sell, nobody needs photos of them, robot or not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time to build anything, and the rent's all mine. What would help is a year of support while you retrain, and help finding the jobs that still exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how lonely it would be. I live by myself, so losing work isn't only money, it's losing the office and the jokes. I'd miss Tunde's terrible puns, and five-a-side on Thursdays would matter a lot more.

headlineQuote: I live by myself, so losing work isn't only money, it's losing the office and the jokes.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old junior designer** at Northpoint, making brochures for estate agents.
He lives **alone** and carries the whole rent, with about four months saved.
He **watches others first** and uses AI tools now and then.
His escape route is **property photography**, the hands-on part of his job.
Ten years makes him **calm**, while two leaves no time to build anything.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: A **year of support** while retraining, and help finding jobs that still exist.
